groups: Who owns the ground in front of you

ground.label: The sidewalk in front of your building
ground.answer: City owns it. You probably pay to fix it.
ground.what: The sidewalk is public right of way owned by the city, but Chicago does not routinely replace residential sidewalk on its own dime. The main path to a new one is the Shared Cost Sidewalk Program, a voluntary CDOT programme where the property owner pays roughly half. Applications open through 311 early in the year and fill within days. Seniors and people with disabilities get a 50 percent discount. Vaulted sidewalks are not eligible. A mid-block property typically runs several hundred to fifteen hundred dollars, and corner lots pay for both sides.

ground.label: Snow on that sidewalk
ground.answer: Yours, by ordinance, with a clock on it.
ground.what: Municipal Code 4-4-310 and 10-8-180 make the abutting owner, lessee or tenant responsible. If snow stops before 4pm you have three hours to clear it, except Sundays. If it stops after 4pm or on a Sunday you have until 10am the next day. The path must be five feet wide where conditions allow. Corner lots must clear every side plus the corner ramps. Fines run from fifty to five hundred dollars, set case by case by an administrative hearings judge. Bus shelters are cleared by the city's contractor; a bus stop without a shelter is on the adjacent owner like any other sidewalk.

ground.label: The parkway, that grass strip at the curb
ground.what: The strip between sidewalk and curb is city right of way, not your lot, even though it sits inside your fence line in some blocks and you are expected to keep it cut. You cannot pave it or build on it without a permit. During sidewalk construction any pavers, planters or fencing you put there may be pulled out and only loosely reset, and putting them back is on you.
contacts: Parkway and right of way permits

ground.label: The tree in the parkway
ground.what: Parkway trees belong to the city, not the adjacent owner, and removing or heavily pruning one without permission is a violation. Trims, removals and new plantings all queue through 311 and land in your forestry district. Chicago has historically removed far more trees than it replants, and a removal does not automatically generate a planting request. That gap is worth watching on your own block.
contacts: Request a tree trim or planting

ground.label: The street surface and its potholes
ground.what: CDOT owns the roadway. Potholes reported to 311 are assigned to the asphalt district, not your ward, and are patched by crews working a queue rather than a route. Full resurfacing is a separate capital decision, and on residential streets it is often paid for out of your alderman's annual menu money rather than a citywide programme.

ground.label: The curb, gutter and your driveway apron
ground.answer: CDOT owns it, you may pay for it.
ground.what: Curb and gutter repair is CDOT work and is frequently bundled into a resurfacing or a shared cost sidewalk job rather than done on its own. A residential driveway apron crossing the sidewalk is permitted to you and maintained at your cost. An abandoned apron gets torn out and replaced with topsoil, billed at the same rate as sidewalk, with no grass seed.

ground.label: The alley behind you
ground.answer: CDOT paves it, Streets and San empties it.
ground.what: Chicago has more alley miles than any city in the world and they are public right of way. CDOT handles the paving, including the Green Alley programme's permeable rebuilds. Streets and Sanitation runs the carts and the rodent baiting. Lighting in the alley is CDOT electrical. Three departments, one strip of pavement, and no single number to call.

ground.label: The street light and alley light
ground.what: Street lights, alley lights and traffic signals are all CDOT electrical district work orders. Chicago finished a citywide LED conversion that also put smart controllers on most poles, so an outage is often detected before anyone reports it. Reporting it anyway creates the ticket that lets you track a fix.

ground.label: Street signs and parking signs
ground.answer: CDOT signs, but your alderman orders them.
ground.what: Stop signs, speed humps, permit parking zones, honorary street names and no-parking restrictions are installed by CDOT but almost always originate as an aldermanic request or a City Council ordinance. This is why a speed hump petition goes to the ward office rather than to 311, and why two adjacent blocks can have completely different parking rules.

ground.label: Everything under the street
ground.what: Water mains, sewers, hydrants, catch basins, B-boxes and the lead service line running into your building are the Department of Water Management's. The city has been replacing lead service lines under a long consent-driven programme, and free water testing kits are available to any resident. A sunken patch of street is usually a collapsed sewer or a water main repair rather than a paving failure.

ground.label: Street cleaning and the ticket
ground.what: Sweeping runs by ward and section from roughly April into November. Temporary signs go up the day before and the ticket is real. The 44th Ward office publishes the section schedule and you can sign up for address-level alerts through the city rather than guessing from the signs.

ground.label: Graffiti on your building or the pole outside
ground.what: Streets and Sanitation removes graffiti free on most surfaces, dispatched by graffiti district. Private property needs an owner consent form on file, which is the step most people miss. Painted-over brick often cannot be restored, so reporting quickly matters more than reporting thoroughly.

ground.label: Rats in the alley
ground.answer: Bureau of Rodent Control, by request.
ground.what: Baiting is complaint-driven rather than scheduled, so a block gets attention roughly in proportion to how often it complains. Crews bait burrows in the alley and parkway. Uncontained garbage is the underlying cause in almost every case, which is why a rat request often generates a sanitation inspection of the same block.

ground.label: The parks
ground.answer: A separate government you also pay taxes to.
ground.what: The Chicago Park District is not a city department. It is an independent unit of local government with its own board of seven commissioners appointed by the mayor and confirmed by City Council, its own budget, its own bonds and its own line on your property tax bill. Day to day maintenance is Park District staff. The community voice is the Park Advisory Council, a registered volunteer body attached to an individual park, of which there are roughly two hundred citywide. A PAC gets free use of the fieldhouse room, waived permit fees and expedited event permits, which makes it the cheapest available lever on a specific park.

ground.label: The lakefront and the beaches
ground.what: The lakefront parks east of Lake Shore Drive are Park District land, but the shoreline itself is bound up with the Army Corps of Engineers, the state's public trust doctrine and a century of Montgomery Ward litigation that keeps it 'forever open, clear and free'. Beach seasons, lifeguards and harbours are Park District; erosion and revetment work usually is not.

unmapped.label: Cook County Commissioner
unmapped.what: The county runs the health system, the jail, the courts, the forest preserves and the assessment of your property. Its districts are not published in the city's GIS.

unmapped.label: Metropolitan Water Reclamation District
unmapped.what: A separate unit of government with its own property tax levy that handles stormwater and sewage treatment for most of Cook County. There is no district to sit inside: every voter in the county votes for all nine commissioners, which is why almost nobody can name one.

unmapped.label: Cook County Board of Review
unmapped.what: Hears property assessment appeals. Its three districts are drawn by the county, not the city.

unmapped.label: Judicial subcircuit
unmapped.what: Circuit Court of Cook County judges are elected from subcircuits drawn by the state legislature. These appear on your ballot and almost never in public maps.

unmapped.label: Chicago Board of Education district
unmapped.what: Chicago's school board became partly elected in 2024 and fully elected in 2026. The twenty districts are drawn by the state and are not yet in the city's open GIS.

layers.label: Ward
layers.what: Your alderman signs off on zoning changes, liquor licenses, driveway permits and sidewalk cafes on your block, and directs the ward's annual infrastructure menu money. A request routed through the ward office usually moves faster than the same request filed cold with 311.

layers.label: Voting precinct
layers.what: The smallest election unit in the city. It sets your polling place and which local races appear on your ballot. Petition drives and campaign canvassing are organized precinct by precinct.

layers.label: Illinois House
layers.what: State law reaches further into daily life than most people expect: school funding, CTA and Metra budgets, tenant protections, the criminal code and the property tax cycle all start in Springfield.

layers.label: Illinois Senate
layers.what: Each Illinois Senate district contains exactly two House districts. Yours holds House 11 and House 12, so your senator's territory is twice your representative's.

layers.label: U.S. Congress
layers.what: Federal money for transit, housing vouchers, the lakefront and disaster response arrives through this office. Casework staff also handle passports, visas, Social Security and VA problems.

layers.label: Community area
layers.what: One of 77 fixed community areas drawn by University of Chicago sociologists in the 1920s. They never change, which is exactly why almost every city statistic is reported at this level. Nearly any Chicago dataset you compare over time is aggregated here.

layers.label: Neighborhood
layers.what: An informal layer with no legal power. The city's file has not been updated since the neighborhood renamed itself Northalsted in 2020, so the official GIS still returns the old name.

layers.label: Census tract
layers.what: The Census Bureau's basic reporting unit, roughly 4,000 people. Federal funding formulas, redistricting, flood insurance and most demographic research run on tract numbers.

layers.label: ZIP code
layers.what: A postal delivery route, not a place. ZIPs cut across wards, community areas and school boundaries, which is why ZIP-level statistics tend to mislead.

layers.label: Zoning district
layers.what: Sets what can legally be built next door: how many units, how tall, how far back from the lot line, how much parking. RM-5 is dense multi-unit residential. Changing it on a single parcel requires an ordinance passed by City Council, which in practice means your alderman's approval.

layers.label: ADU zone
layers.what: Coach houses and basement apartments are pre-approved in this zone rather than requiring a variance. The pilot program was expanded citywide after years of pressure, and the 44th Ward office was one of its more active backers.

layers.label: Affordable Requirements zone
layers.what: Any new development of ten or more units here must include affordable units on site or pay into a fund. Inclusionary Areas carry a higher on-site requirement than the rest of the city.

layers.label: Pedestrian street
layers.what: A designation that bans drive-throughs, blank walls and street-facing parking lots, forcing storefronts to meet the sidewalk. Broadway and Clark carry it in stretches.

layers.label: Planned development
layers.what: A Planned Development replaces standard zoning with a negotiated, site-specific deal. Large projects near Wrigley Field are built under these.

layers.label: Historic district
layers.what: Landmark and historic districts require Commission on Chicago Landmarks review before exterior work. Alta Vista Terrace, four blocks north, is the nearest.

layers.label: TIF district
layers.what: Inside a TIF, property tax revenue above a frozen 1990s-era baseline is diverted from schools, parks and the county into a district account for local capital projects. This one funds the Red and Purple Line rebuild. It is the single least visible thing on your tax bill.

properties.n: Red and Purple Modernization Phase One Project

layers.label: Special Service Area
layers.what: An extra property tax levy that funds sidewalk power washing, planters, banners, holiday lights, supplemental snow removal and street festivals, spent by a local chamber of commerce rather than the city. Your address is not inside one. SSA #8 (Lakeview East) and SSA #18 (Northalsted) both stop within a few blocks.

layers.label: Police district
layers.what: The 19th District, Town Hall, runs from Lawrence to Fullerton, the lake to the river. Station at 850 W Addison. This is the level with a commander, a front desk and a district council.

layers.label: Police beat
layers.what: The smallest patrol unit, and the level CAPS community meetings are organized around. Beat meetings run roughly ten times a year at 6:30pm and are the most direct way to raise a recurring block-level problem.

layers.label: Detective area
layers.what: Detective divisions work at the area level, not the district. Area 3 handles investigations for several districts including the 19th.

layers.label: CPS elementary boundary
layers.what: Nettelhorst is your guaranteed-seat neighborhood elementary school, K through 8. Attendance boundary means a right to enroll, not a requirement, and a large share of CPS students attend somewhere else through choice, magnet or selective programs.

layers.label: CPS high school boundary
layers.what: Lake View High School is your guaranteed-seat neighborhood high school. Selective enrollment and magnet high schools admit citywide and ignore this boundary entirely.

layers.label: Sanitation division
layers.what: Streets and Sanitation splits the city into divisions above the ward level for crew assignment. This is internal plumbing, invisible on any public-facing map, but it determines which yard your garbage truck rolls out of.

layers.label: Sanitation district
layers.what: The district your sanitation crews report to. Escalating a missed pickup past 311 usually means getting the ward office to call this district directly.

layers.label: Garbage pickup day
layers.what: Black cart collection day for your grid. Streets and Sanitation runs a grid system rather than a ward system, which was the big 2012 reform: crews now work contiguous geography instead of ward boundaries, and the ward you live in no longer determines your pickup day.

layers.label: Alley collection block
layers.what: The internal Streets and Sanitation alley block record for your block. It carries the collection day, the number of carts the city thinks are back there, and the truck number assigned to it. This is operational plumbing, not something the city publishes for residents, and it is the most specific thing about your address in this whole file.
contacts: Report a cart or alley issue

layers.label: Recycling route
layers.what: Which week your blue cart is collected and who drives the truck. Chicago splits recycling between city crews and private haulers by zone. This zone is served by city crews, which historically have had a lower contamination-rejection rate than some contracted areas.

layers.label: Forestry district
layers.what: Where a tree trim, tree removal or parkway planting request is queued. Bureau of Forestry crews are assigned by district, and backlogs vary sharply between them.

layers.label: Graffiti removal district
layers.what: Graffiti Blasters crews are dispatched by district. A removal request filed at 311 lands in this district's queue and is typically handled within a couple of weeks on public-facing surfaces.

layers.label: Snow section
layers.what: Snow plowing is organized into districts, then sections, then routes. Main arterials are cleared first by section, residential side streets only after. Your section number determines the order.

layers.label: Street sweeping section
layers.what: Street sweeping is scheduled by ward and section, roughly April through November. Sections are posted with temporary signs the day before and the ticket for ignoring them is real.

layers.label: CDOT asphalt district
layers.what: CDOT splits pothole and resurfacing crews into districts. A pothole reported at 311 is assigned here, not to your ward.

layers.label: CDOT electrical district
layers.what: Street lights, alley lights and traffic signals are maintained by CDOT electrical district. A light out on your block is this district's work order.

layers.label: Water district
layers.what: The Department of Water Management divides the city into sections for main breaks, hydrant work and meter service. Water quality complaints and lead service line questions route through here.

layers.label: Park district park
layers.what: Chicago Park District land is a separate unit of government with its own board, budget and property tax levy. Your address is not inside a park polygon. Gill Park at Broadway and Sheridan is the nearest fieldhouse.

layers.label: Green alley rebuilds
layers.what: Green Alley projects rebuild the alley with permeable surfaces so stormwater soaks in instead of overwhelming the sewer. Most were paid for with a mix of TIF and aldermanic menu money.

layers.label: Bike routes
layers.what: Marked bike infrastructure, from protected lanes to shared-lane markings. The classification matters: a painted sharrow and a concrete-protected lane are both drawn as a bike route.

layers.label: Winter snow routes
layers.what: Designated arterial snow routes. Parking is banned on these streets from December 1 to April 1 between 3am and 7am regardless of whether snow has fallen, and cars are towed.

layers.label: CTA rail lines
layers.what: CTA rail alignment. The Red Line runs in the embankment through Lakeview and the Red and Purple Modernization project rebuilt these tracks and stations, funded in part by the TIF your address sits in.

layers.label: Packaged liquor restricted
layers.what: Street segments where packaged-goods liquor sales are restricted by ordinance, usually the result of a precinct vote or an aldermanic moratorium. A genuinely Chicago layer: prohibition survives block by block.

layers.label: Tavern moratorium
layers.what: Street segments under a tavern licence moratorium. New bars cannot open on these blocks without City Council lifting the restriction, which is why some corridors have a fixed number of bars for decades.

layers.label: CTA stations
layers.what: Rail stations near the address. Addison, Belmont and Sheridan are the closest Red Line stops.

layers.label: Public library
layers.what: Chicago Public Library is a city department, not a district, so there is no boundary to fall inside. The John Merlo branch on Belmont is the nearest, and branch meeting rooms are free to reserve for community meetings.

nearest.label: Nearest park
nearest.what: Park District land, with its official class and acreage. Mini-parks under an acre get no fieldhouse and no staff; neighbourhood parks do. Class is what determines programming, not size alone.

nearest.label: Nearest police station
nearest.what: The district station house with a front desk, a commander and a district council. Reports can be filed here in person or online for many non-violent incidents.

nearest.label: Nearest fire house
nearest.what: Chicago Fire Department engine and truck companies respond by closest-unit dispatch, not by district boundary, so this is a good proxy for response time but not a guarantee of who arrives.

nearest.label: Nearest library branch
nearest.what: Chicago Public Library branches have free meeting rooms you can reserve, which makes them the default venue for block club and PAC meetings in this neighbourhood.

nearest.label: Nearest CTA rail station
nearest.what: Rail access shapes zoning here: transit-served parcels qualify for reduced parking minimums and denser development under the city's transit-oriented development rules.

nearest.label: Nearest hospital
nearest.what: Emergency ambulance routing is by availability and specialty, not proximity, so the closest hospital is not necessarily where you would be taken.

nearest.label: Nearest post office
nearest.what: Retail postal unit. ZIP boundaries are drawn around delivery routes from units like this one, which is why ZIPs ignore every other boundary on this map.

nearest.label: Your ward office
nearest.what: The physical office where service requests, permits and complaints are handled in person. Open weekdays, 9 to 5.

nearest.label: Nearest public health site
nearest.what: Chicago Department of Public Health clinics and partner sites, covering immunisation, sexual health and mental health services on a sliding scale.
